title: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
summary: Why the best score on a reused query set is inflated, and how query splits, rotating sealed sets, bootstrap CIs, multiple-comparison correction and contamination checks keep search evals honest.
outcomes: Explain why the best of N systems on a fixed query set scores too high, and estimate the inflation from N and n
Explain adaptive overfitting, the boosting attack and how the Ladder and Thresholdout limit leakage
Design query-level train, dev and sealed test splits that rotate on a schedule
Compute a paired bootstrap CI over queries and apply Bonferroni or Holm to a family of tests
Recognize contamination paths in search and LLM evals and choose a defense

lessons.title: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high

blocks.md:
You have a search system and a **public query set**: 50 queries with relevance labels that everyone on the team can score against. You try a new prompt, a new BM25 weight, a new reranker threshold, and keep whatever scores best. Months later the shipped system does worse on real traffic than the public number promised.

This course explains why that happens and how to stop it. The short version: picking the maximum of many noisy scores is itself a form of fitting, and the query set is the training data for that fit.

Recall from the overfitting lesson: a model overfits when it learns noise in its training data that does not repeat on new data. Here the "model" is your choice of system, and the "training data" is the public query set. Each query's score depends partly on how good the system really is and partly on luck: which queries happen to be in the set and how this particular system's quirks line up with them.

To see the effect with nothing else going on, we built a toy (simplified on purpose). Every system scores a query with nDCG@10 drawn as

- a shared query difficulty (standard deviation 0.15, the same for every system), plus
- a system-specific wobble (standard deviation 0.15, different per system and per query),

added to 0.40 and clipped to [0, 1]. Every system has **exactly the same true quality**: an expected nDCG@10 of 0.402 (estimated from 2 million draws). Any system that looks better is lucky.

blocks.prompt: You evaluate 100 such systems on the 50 public queries and pick the best one. Then you score that winner on 50 fresh queries it has never seen. What do you expect for the winner's public score and its fresh score?
blocks.reveal: Averaged over 1,000 repeats of the experiment, the winner of 100 scores **0.455** on the public set and **0.402** on fresh queries. The public number is inflated by 0.053 nDCG, about 13 percent relative, and the whole gain is luck. On the fresh set the winner is exactly as good as every other system, because they were all identical.

blocks.title: One run: 200 identical systems, the top 5 on the public set

scenes.caption: Ground truth. All 200 systems have the same expected nDCG@10 of 0.402. Nothing distinguishes them except noise.
Scores on the 50 public queries. The top five range from 0.444 down to 0.426 while the median of all 200 is 0.391. System 34 looks like a clear win.
The same five on 50 fresh queries: 0.398, 0.378, 0.423, 0.414, 0.379. The public ranking does not carry over and the winner falls back to the pack.

blocks.md: Notice that this particular public set was a bit hard (the median system scored 0.391, below the true 0.402). The absolute level of a query set moves every system together. What matters for selection is the **spread between systems** on the same queries, and that spread is pure noise here.

blocks.title: Best of N systems, averaged over 1,000 repeats

scenes.caption: Public score of the best of N systems. Trying more systems pushes the winner's public score up: 0.403, 0.427, 0.440, 0.455, 0.465.
Fresh score of the same winners: 0.402, 0.401, 0.401, 0.402, 0.403. The more you search, the bigger the gap, while the real quality never moves.

blocks.md: Why does the gap grow with N? Each system's public mean is the true mean plus noise with some standard deviation $\sigma$. The best of N noisy numbers is the true mean plus the **maximum** of N noise draws, and the expected maximum grows with N. For Gaussian noise there is a clean upper bound.

blocks.caption: s is the per-query spread between systems on the same query (0.146 in our toy) and n is the number of queries. With n = 50, sigma is about 0.021.

blocks.title: How much inflation to expect from picking the best of N

curves.label: upper bound s/sqrt(n) x sqrt(2 ln N)

scenes.caption: With 50 queries the bound gives 0.063 at N = 100 and 0.073 at N = 500. The simulated inflation (dots, 50 queries) sits just under it: 0.053 and 0.063.
Ten times more queries shrinks the bound by sqrt(10): about 0.020 at N = 100. In the simulation, the best of 100 on 500 queries is inflated by 0.017. (The dots stay at their 50-query values.)
A noisier metric or a more diverse query set (larger s) inflates the winner more for the same N and n. A binary per-query metric such as precision@1 can be noisier still.

blocks.md: The curse also hides real gains. In the same toy we planted one system that is **truly better by +0.03** among 199 identical ones. With 50 queries it came out on top in only 11.8 percent of 1,000 runs; with 500 queries it won 94 percent of 300 runs. A small query set is noisy enough that the selection step mostly picks luck.

The maximum of many noisy scores is biased upward. Selecting a system on a query set uses up that set: its score for the winner is no longer an unbiased estimate. The bias grows with the number of systems tried (roughly like sqrt(ln N)) and shrinks with more queries (like 1/sqrt(n)).

Misconception: "we never trained on the test queries, so the number is clean." Choosing among variants by their test score is training with a very small model: one decision per comparison. A hundred prompt tweaks checked against the same 50 queries is a hundred-way fit.

blocks.question: A teammate tried 40 reranker configurations on a 50-query public set and reports the best one improved nDCG@10 by +0.035 over the baseline. What is the most defensible next step?
options: Ship it, since +0.035 is larger than typical noise on 50 queries
Re-run the same 40 configurations on the same 50 queries with a different random seed to confirm
Score only the chosen configuration (and the baseline) once on a fresh query set that played no part in the choice
Report the average of all 40 configurations instead of the best one
blocks.explain: The +0.035 is a maximum over 40 noisy comparisons, so it is biased upward. In our toy, the best of 20 identical systems already gains about +0.038 on 50 queries from luck alone. Re-running on the same queries cannot remove that selection bias, and averaging all 40 answers a different question. A single evaluation on untouched queries gives an unbiased estimate.

blocks.question: In the toy, what happens to the expected inflation of the best-of-100 winner if you keep N = 100 but grow the public set from 50 to 200 queries?
options: It roughly halves, because the noise in each system's mean scales like 1/sqrt(n)
It drops to about a quarter, because inflation scales like 1/n
It stays the same, because the number of systems is unchanged
It grows, because more queries give more chances to get lucky
blocks.explain: Each system's mean has noise of about s/sqrt(n). Four times as many queries halves that standard deviation, and the expected maximum of 100 draws halves with it. Selection bias shrinks with more queries but never vanishes while you keep selecting.

lessons.title: Adaptive overfitting: how score feedback leaks the test set

blocks.md: Lesson 1 picked the best of a fixed pool. Real work is worse: you look at the score, then design the next system **because of** that score. Roelofs et al. call this **adaptive overfitting**: overfitting caused by reusing a test set, where each new model depends on what earlier test scores revealed.

Recht et al. split the drop you see when moving from an old test set $S$ to a new one $S'$ into three parts. $L$ is the loss of the chosen model, $D$ the distribution behind $S$, and $D'$ the distribution behind the new set.

blocks.tex: L_S - L_{S'} = \underbrace{(L_S - L_D)}_{\text{adaptivity gap}} + \underbrace{(L_D - L_{D'})}_{\text{distribution gap}} + \underbrace{(L_{D'} - L_{S'})}_{\text{generalization gap}}
blocks.caption: The adaptivity gap is what tuning on S bought you that the population does not give back. The distribution gap is a real shift between old and new data. The generalization gap is ordinary sampling noise on S'.

blocks.md:
How far can feedback alone go? Blum and Hardt describe a **boosting attack** on a leaderboard that reports exact scores. In our search version, each of the 50 public queries has two candidate documents and the metric is precision@1: did the system put the relevant one first? An attacker who knows nothing submits random choices:

1. Submit k random rankings and read each public score.
2. Keep the ones that scored at least 0.5.
3. Per query, take the majority choice among the kept rankings and submit that.

blocks.prompt: The attacker never sees a single label. With k = 300 submissions, what public precision@1 does the majority vote reach on the 50 public queries, and what does it score on 50 fresh queries?
blocks.reveal: Averaged over 400 simulated runs: **0.907** on the public queries and **0.498** on fresh ones, which is coin flipping. Each kept ranking agrees with the hidden labels slightly more than chance, and the majority vote stacks those small biases. Score feedback alone lifted public precision@1 by about 0.4 on exactly those 50 queries and nothing else.

blocks.title: Boosting attack on a 50-query leaderboard (400 runs each)

scenes.caption: Exact scores revealed. The public precision@1 of the majority vote climbs with the number of submissions: 0.595, 0.660, 0.769, 0.907, 0.991.
The same final rankings on 50 fresh queries: 0.500, 0.499, 0.502, 0.498, 0.496. True quality is exactly chance, as it must be.
Same attack against the parameter-free Ladder (below). Few submissions ever count as improvements (about 2.5 on average at k = 1000), so the vote reaches only 0.547 to 0.621.

blocks.md: The **Ladder** (Blum and Hardt, ICML 2015) changes what the leaderboard reveals. It only reports a new score when a submission beats the best so far by a margin; otherwise it repeats the old best. The parameter-free version picks the margin with a paired test: the standard deviation $s$ of the per-example difference between the new submission and the current best, divided by $\sqrt{n}$. Released scores are rounded to a multiple of $1/n$. Below we write it for a higher-is-better metric (the paper uses losses) and run it on five submissions of the toy nDCG systems.

blocks.title: Parameter-free Ladder on five submissions (n = 50 queries)
blocks.code:
import statistics as st

def ladder(submissions, n):
    shown = float('-inf')         # public score
    best = [0.0] * n               # per-query scores of best
    for scores in submissions:     # one list per run
        mean = sum(scores) / n
        diff = [a - b for a, b in zip(scores, best)]
        s = st.stdev(diff)
        if mean > shown + s / n ** 0.5:
            shown = round(mean * n) / n   # round to 1/n
            best = scores
        yield shown

scenes.caption: Submission 1 (true quality 0.402) scores 0.424. Nothing beats minus infinity, so it is accepted and shown rounded to 0.42.
Submission 2 is another null tweak at 0.420. The margin s/sqrt(n) = 0.200/7.07 = 0.028 puts the bar at 0.448, so the leaderboard repeats 0.42 and reveals nothing new.
Submission 3 is truly better by +0.03 and scores 0.458, above the bar of 0.450. It becomes the new best and 0.46 is shown.
Submission 4, a null tweak, scores 0.399 against a bar of 0.492. Rejected: the team learns only that it did not clearly beat 0.46.
Submission 5 is truly better by +0.06 and scores 0.544, above 0.488. Accepted and shown as 0.54. Real gains still get through; small noisy wiggles do not.

blocks.md: Blum and Hardt prove the Ladder's leaderboard error is at most on the order of $(\log(k)/n)^{1/3}$ for $k$ adaptively chosen submissions, while a leaderboard that releases precise scores can be driven to error on the order of $\sqrt{k/n}$ by the boosting attack. Kaggle's mitigation at the time was mainly to limit the rate of resubmission and the precision of released scores, and rank the final standings on a separate **private** split that is never shown during the competition.

How much does adaptive overfitting hurt in practice? The evidence is reassuring for large test sets:

- Recht et al. built new test sets for CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. Accuracy fell 3 to 15 percent on CIFAR-10 and 11 to 14 percent on ImageNet, but models that were better on the old set were even better on the new one (no diminishing returns). They attribute the drop to slightly harder images, a distribution gap, not to adaptivity.
- Roelofs et al. compared public and private leaderboards in 120 Kaggle competitions and found little evidence of substantial overfitting; effects among top submissions were typically under 1 percent accuracy. The outliers had pathologies such as non-i.i.d. splits or effectively small test sets.

Do not read those results as "test reuse is safe." ImageNet's test set has tens of thousands of images and Kaggle private splits often thousands of rows. Search teams often tune against 50 to 200 queries with free-form changes (prompts, thresholds, filters). That is exactly the small-n, many-k regime where the toy overfits.

blocks.question: A leaderboard shows exact scores to five decimals, allows 10 submissions a day, and has a 60-query public set. Which change most directly limits how much label information each submission leaks?
options: Raise the daily cap to 50 so teams stop hoarding submissions
Show a new score only when a submission beats the current best by a significance margin, otherwise repeat the old best
Switch the metric from nDCG@10 to MRR
Publish the per-query scores so teams can debug faster
blocks.explain: That is the Ladder idea. Most submissions then reveal nothing beyond "not a clear improvement", which caps what an adaptive analyst can learn about the hidden labels. More submissions or per-query scores leak more, and changing the metric does not change the leakage.

blocks.question: Recht et al. saw an 11 to 14 percent ImageNet accuracy drop on a new test set, yet concluded adaptive overfitting was not the main cause. Which observation supports that?
options: The drop was the same for every model
The new test set was smaller than the original
Gains on the original test set translated into larger gains on the new one, with no diminishing returns for the most-tuned models
Models trained longer dropped the most
blocks.explain: If years of tuning had fit the old test set, the most-tuned recent models would gain little on new data. Instead accuracy on the new set followed a line with slope above 1 against the old accuracy. The authors attribute the gap mainly to the new images being slightly harder, a distribution gap.

lessons.title: Split by query and keep a rotating sealed test set

blocks.md: A search system generalizes to **new queries**, so the query is the unit you hold out. Relevance labels usually come as (query, document, grade) rows. If you shuffle rows into train and test, the same query lands on both sides: the system can memorize what was relevant for that query during training and get credit for it at test time.

blocks.title: 24 judged pairs from 8 queries: split by pair vs by query

scenes.caption: Eight queries, three judged documents each. We want a 75/25 split: 18 pairs for training, 6 for testing.
Random split by pair (one fixed seed). The 6 test pairs (red) come from q1, q3, q4, q6 and q7, and every one of those queries also has pairs in training.
Over 100,000 random pair splits, 96 percent of test pairs have their query in training. Split by query instead: all of q4 and q7 go to test (green) and no test query was ever seen.

blocks.md: Splitting by query is necessary but not sufficient. Logs contain near-duplicates ("reset router" and "how to reset my router"), so group paraphrases and normalized duplicates into clusters first and split by **cluster**. Also split by time when you can: train and tune on older queries, test on newer ones, so tomorrow's traffic is what you measure.

blocks.title: Where each query set sits and who may look at it

scenes.caption: Queries come from logs, are clustered so paraphrases stay together, then split by cluster.
The team iterates against dev as often as it likes. Dev scores will be optimistic for the final choice, and that is expected.
The sealed test set is read rarely, for a pre-declared comparison, with every read logged. Each read spends some of its trustworthiness.

blocks.md: Fuhr (SIGIR Forum 2017) adds two warnings from IR practice. Any tuning set must be disjoint from the test set, and comparing against "the best published run" on a collection is itself a tuning step. Fuhr also notes a single holdout split can be unreliable: in a reproducibility study the paper cites, performance on the two halves of a collection differed by 20 percent, so cross-validation over query folds is a sensible minimum when data is scarce.

Their private-leaderboard check is a good template. The top public run, measured on 5,793 public queries, was ranked fourth in expectation on the 45 private queries (MRR with MS MARCO labels) and fifth or sixth with TREC labels. With only 45 queries the private ranks are spread out, so this is a warning sign to investigate rather than proof of overfitting. They call TREC's single-shot submission on fresh queries each year the gold standard for avoiding reuse, and a freely reused test collection the worst case.

blocks.title: A rotating sealed test set (one possible schedule)

scenes.caption: Quarter 1: set A is open for tuning, set B is sealed, and set C is being sampled from recent logs and labeled.
Quarter 2: B has been read for one release decision, so it is opened for tuning. C becomes the sealed test set and D starts labeling.

Each quarter the cycle repeats. Every sealed set is read for a few decisions only, then retired to dev, so no test score is the product of months of peeking. Fresh sets also track drift in real traffic.

blocks.md: If you cannot afford fresh labels often, you can make one holdout last longer. **Thresholdout** (Dwork, Feldman, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold and Roth; Science 2015) answers each query with the *training* score unless training and holdout disagree by more than a noisy threshold $T$; only then does it reveal the holdout score plus noise, and it spends one unit of a budget $B$. Most answers therefore leak almost nothing about the holdout. In their synthetic test (10,000 points, 10,000 random features, no real signal), reusing a plain holdout for feature selection reported over 63 percent accuracy where 50 percent is the truth; Thresholdout reported values near the truth.

Hold out queries, not pairs, and cluster near-duplicates before splitting. Tune on dev as much as you like, read the sealed test set rarely and for decisions you declared in advance, and replace it on a schedule.

blocks.question: Your team trains a learned reranker on click logs from January to June and evaluates on 300 labeled queries sampled from the same months. Which leak is most likely to inflate the test score?
options: The test queries use graded rather than binary labels
Many test queries, or close paraphrases of them, also appear in the training clicks
The test set is too large for a bootstrap confidence interval
The reranker uses a cross-encoder instead of a bi-encoder
blocks.explain: Popular queries repeat. A reranker trained on clicks for a query has effectively seen its answer. Split by query cluster and preferably by time (train on earlier months, test on later), so test queries are genuinely new.

blocks.question: Why does the MS MARCO document leaderboard score every submission on 45 extra queries that never appear on the public board?
options: To give the organizers a held-out check on whether public gains carry over to queries no one could tune on
To raise the total number of evaluation queries so the public score is more precise
Because TREC labels are too expensive to show publicly
To break ties on the public leaderboard
blocks.explain: A private set that no participant receives feedback on cannot be adaptively overfit. If teams were climbing the public board by tuning to its queries, their runs would gain publicly and slip on the private queries.

lessons.title: Confidence intervals by bootstrapping over queries

blocks.md: A single number like "B beats A by +0.030 nDCG@10" hides how much it would move with a different sample of queries. A **confidence interval** (CI) gives a range of plausible values for the true difference. Sakai (SIGIR Forum 2014) argues IR papers should report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not just p-values, because a p-value mixes the size of the effect with the number of topics.

Since queries are the sampling unit, resample **queries**. Take the per-query differences $d_i = B_i - A_i$. Draw $n$ queries with replacement from the $n$ you have, average their differences, and repeat thousands of times. The spread of those averages approximates how the mean difference would vary across fresh query samples. This is the **percentile bootstrap**.

scenes.caption: Per-query differences for 10 queries (the first 10 of our 50). Their mean is +0.070. Note the large spread: B loses badly on queries 0 and 2 and wins big on 6 and 7.
Resample 1 draws query indices 9, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 8, 2, 9, 8. Queries 2 and 9 appear twice, 8 three times, and others not at all. Mean: +0.092.
Resample 2 draws 5, 8, 7, 7, 4, 1, 4, 6, 4, 8. Mean: +0.191. A third resample gives +0.064. Repeating this thousands of times traces out the sampling distribution.

blocks.tex: \bar d^{*(b)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_{J_i^{(b)}},\quad J_i^{(b)} \sim \text{Uniform}\{1,\dots,n\};\qquad \text{CI}_{95} = \big[\,q_{0.025}(\bar d^{*}),\; q_{0.975}(\bar d^{*})\,\big]
blocks.caption: Each bootstrap replicate b averages the differences of n queries drawn with replacement. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of B replicates form the 95 percent percentile interval.

blocks.code:
import random

def paired_bootstrap_ci(a, b, reps=10_000, seed=32):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    d = [y - x for x, y in zip(a, b)]   # one difference per query
    n = len(d)
    means = sorted(
        sum(d[rng.randrange(n)] for _ in range(n)) / n
        for _ in range(reps))
    return means[int(0.025 * (reps - 1))], means[int(0.975 * (reps - 1))]
blocks.caption: Resample queries, keep each query's A and B scores together (paired), and read off percentiles.

blocks.md: On the full toy: system A scores 0.425 and system B 0.455 on 50 queries, a difference of +0.030 (B's true advantage is +0.020). Ten thousand paired bootstrap replicates give a 95 percent CI of **[-0.022, +0.081]**. The interval includes 0: with 50 queries we cannot rule out that B is no better, and 12.6 percent of replicates have B not ahead.

blocks.title: 10,000 bootstrap means of B minus A (percent per bin)

scenes.caption: The bootstrap distribution of the mean difference is centered near the observed +0.030 with a standard error of about 0.026.
The first two bins, where B is not ahead, hold about 13 percent of replicates. That is why the 95 percent interval [-0.022, +0.081] crosses zero. More queries would narrow it.

blocks.md: **Pair your resamples.** If you resample A's queries and B's queries independently, the CI widens to [-0.056, +0.115]. Query difficulty affects both systems (their per-query scores correlate at 0.64 here), and pairing cancels it, leaving only the differences that matter. The Ladder's parameter-free margin in lesson 2 uses a paired statistic for the same reason.

blocks.prompt: You compute a 95 percent bootstrap CI for the **winner** of 100 identical systems from lesson 1, using the same 50 public queries you selected it on. How often does that interval contain the winner's true score of 0.402?
blocks.reveal: In 400 simulated runs, only **60.5 percent** of the time, versus 93.5 percent for a system picked at random from the same pool. The bootstrap assumes the queries were not used to choose the system. After selection the interval is centered on an inflated mean, so it misses the truth far more than 5 percent of the time.

blocks.md: A confidence interval or significance test computed on the same queries you used to pick the winner is not valid. Report CIs from a set that played no part in the choice.

Bootstrapping also answers "how stable is this leaderboard?" MS MARCO's organizers resampled the query set 1,000 times and re-ranked the runs each time. On the public boards the first-ranked run never fell below third, while the fifth-ranked run held fifth place less than half the time: close runs are effectively tied. Lin et al. add that new state-of-the-art claims on the MS MARCO document leaderboard are almost never qualified with significance testing.

Resample queries, keep each query's pair of scores together, and report the interval along with the mean. A CI that crosses zero means your query set cannot tell the systems apart, whatever the point estimate says.

blocks.question: Two systems' per-query nDCG@10 values correlate at 0.9 across 100 queries. Compared with an unpaired bootstrap, what does a paired bootstrap of the mean difference give?
options: A wider interval, because pairing loses degrees of freedom
The same interval, because the means are identical either way
A much narrower interval, because shared query difficulty cancels in the per-query differences
An interval centered on a different value
blocks.explain: The point estimate is the same mean difference either way. With strong correlation, most per-query variation is query difficulty that hits both systems alike. Differencing per query removes it, so the variance of the difference is much smaller than the sum of the two variances.

lessons.title: Testing many variants: Bonferroni and Holm corrections

blocks.md: A significance test at level $\alpha = 0.05$ promises that **one** comparison of two equal systems is declared different only 5 percent of the time. Compare 20 variants against a baseline and that promise no longer covers the set: some null variant will often cross the line by luck. The chance of at least one false discovery across a family of tests is the **familywise error rate** (FWER).

Sakai gives the IR version. Comparing $m = 10$ systems pairwise means 45 tests; if they were independent at $\alpha = 0.05$, the FWER would be $1 - 0.95^{45} = 0.90$. Fuhr adds that reusing a test collection is multiple testing too, and a sequential kind where each test is informed by earlier results.

blocks.title: Familywise error rate for m independent tests

scenes.caption: At alpha 0.05, 20 independent tests give a 0.64 chance of at least one false positive, and 45 tests give 0.90.
Bonferroni tests each at alpha/m, which holds the family's error at or below alpha (the green curve stays under 0.05) for any m.
Lowering alpha to 0.01 helps a single test, but the uncorrected curve still climbs past 0.6 by m = 100. Only the correction scales with m.

blocks.tex: \text{Bonferroni: reject } H_i \text{ if } p_i \le \frac{\alpha}{m}. \qquad \text{Holm: sort } p_{(1)} \le \dots \le p_{(m)};\; \text{reject } H_{(j)} \text{ while } p_{(j)} \le \frac{\alpha}{m - j + 1}
blocks.caption: Holm stops at the first sorted p-value that fails its threshold and accepts the rest. Both control FWER at alpha; Holm rejects everything Bonferroni does and sometimes more.

blocks.md: Now a concrete run. A baseline and 20 variants are scored on the same 50 queries with the toy model. Three variants are truly better (V3 by +0.12, V7 by +0.09, V15 by +0.07); the other 17 are identical to the baseline. Each variant gets a paired t-test against the baseline. The run uses a seed chosen to show all three behaviors at once.

blocks.title: Smallest 8 of 20 p-values, sorted, with Holm thresholds

scenes.caption: Sorted p-values. Uncorrected at 0.05, six variants look significant: V3, V15, V7, V17, V2 and V16.
But V17, V2 and V16 are null variants. They gained +0.060, +0.069 and +0.066 by luck (this baseline drew a hard set of per-query wobbles, which lifts every comparison).
Holm walks down the list: 3e-7 is under 0.0025, 2e-5 under 0.0026, 6e-5 under 0.0028, then 0.0126 exceeds 0.0029 and it stops. Only the three real gains survive.

blocks.md: Over 2,000 simulated repeats with **all 20 variants null**, the chance of at least one false "win" was 0.421 uncorrected, 0.034 with Bonferroni and 0.034 with Holm. It is lower than the independence formula's 0.642 because all tests share one baseline, which correlates them; correction still matters a lot.

Correction has a price. A single real +0.06 variant among 19 null ones was detected 51.9 percent of the time uncorrected, but only 12.4 percent with Bonferroni and 12.5 percent with Holm, because 50 queries give little power. The fix is not to skip correction but to **test fewer things** on the sealed set (one pre-declared comparison) or to **use more queries**. For all-pairs comparisons among many systems, Sakai and Fuhr recommend a multiple-comparison procedure such as (randomized) Tukey HSD.

Count every comparison you make on a query set, including metrics, variants and earlier papers' tests, and correct for the family. Holm is never worse than Bonferroni. Better still, decide the one comparison you will test before you look.

blocks.question: You compare 5 variants to a baseline on the sealed test set. Sorted p-values are 0.004, 0.011, 0.020, 0.030, 0.400. With Holm at FWER 0.05, which variants are declared better?
options: All four with p below 0.05
Only the first (0.004)
None, because 0.004 is above 0.05/5 = 0.01
The first two (0.004 and 0.011)
blocks.explain: Holm thresholds are 0.05/5 = 0.010, 0.05/4 = 0.0125, 0.05/3 = 0.0167, 0.05/2 = 0.025, 0.05. Here 0.004 is at most 0.010 and 0.011 is at most 0.0125, but 0.020 exceeds 0.0167, so Holm stops after two. Bonferroni (every p at most 0.010) would have kept only the first.

blocks.question: Why did the 17 null variants in the concrete run look better than the baseline on average?
options: The paired t-test is biased toward the variant
Every comparison reused the same baseline run, which happened to score low on these queries, so the tests are correlated
Holm correction shifts p-values downward
The variants were trained on the test queries
blocks.explain: The baseline scored 0.357 while its true quality is 0.402. Every variant was compared to that one unlucky draw, so they all looked better together. Shared baselines make multiple tests correlated, which is why the observed FWER (0.421) differs from the independence formula (0.642).

lessons.title: Contamination: when test queries leak into training data

blocks.md: Everything so far assumed the system had never seen the test queries; only its designers had. **Data contamination** breaks that assumption directly. Sainz et al. call the worst kind training a model on the test split of a benchmark and then evaluating it on that benchmark. The result overestimates performance relative to clean models, and the size of the problem is hard to measure.

Search and RAG stacks have several leak paths:

- **Pretraining**: popular benchmarks (MS MARCO, BEIR datasets, QA sets) are published on the web, so an LLM reranker, query rewriter or embedding model may have read the test queries and even the labeled passages.
- **Fine-tuning data**: click logs or synthetic training queries generated from a corpus that contains the test documents.
- **Your own team**: examples copied from the test set into prompts or few-shot demonstrations while debugging.

blocks.title: How a public test set ends up inside the model

scenes.caption: The benchmark is public, so it is mirrored on the web and reused as seeds for synthetic training data.
Both paths feed the training corpus, and the model learns the test queries or their answers.
Evaluating that model on the same benchmark now measures recall of memorized items mixed with real skill.

blocks.md: A toy model shows how little leakage it takes. Suppose a system scores 0.40 nDCG@10 on genuinely new queries but 0.95 on queries it has memorized. If a fraction $c$ of the test set is contaminated, the measured score is $(1 - c) \times 0.40 + c \times 0.95$.

blocks.title: Measured score vs contaminated fraction (toy model)

x.label: fraction of test queries seen in train

scenes.caption: With 10 percent of queries memorized, the measured score is 0.455: the same +0.055 a team would celebrate as a big win, and the same size as the best-of-100 inflation in lesson 1.
Memorization need not be perfect. If memorized queries score only 0.60, 10 percent contamination still adds +0.020, enough to flip a close comparison.

blocks.md:
Evidence from LLM benchmarks shows the effect is real but uneven:

- **GSM1k** (Zhang et al., 2024) wrote 1,205 new grade-school math problems matched to GSM8k's style and difficulty. Some model families dropped by up to 8 percent accuracy, and a model's probability of generating GSM8k examples correlated with its gap (Spearman $r^2 = 0.36$). Many frontier models showed minimal signs of overfitting. GSM1k was withheld from public release at publication to avoid the same fate, with a release precommitted for later.
- **LiveCodeBench** tags every problem with its contest release date, so a model can be scored only on problems released after its training cutoff. DeepSeek, GPT-4o and Codestral dropped sharply on LeetCode problems released after Aug 2023, Oct 2023 and Jan 2024 respectively, around their training cutoffs, which the authors read as likely contamination of the older problems.

Defenses map onto the earlier lessons:

1. **Decontaminate training data**: drop training items with high n-gram overlap with the test set, or that are too close in embedding space (both are common practice, per the GSM1k paper).
2. **Split by time**: evaluate on queries and documents created after the model's training cutoff.
3. **Keep a private set**: unpublished, labeled in-house, refreshed on a schedule (lesson 3), released only after it is retired.
4. **Check external validity**: BEIR evaluates retrievers zero-shot on 18 datasets. Its authors found BM25 a robust baseline, while dense and sparse neural retrievers often underperformed in this zero-shot setting. A gain that holds across domains is harder to fake.

A public benchmark score for a model trained on web-scale data is an upper bound on its skill on your queries, not an estimate. Before trusting a gain, ask whether the model, the synthetic training data or the judge could have seen these queries.

Putting it together: split by query cluster and time, tune on dev, read a sealed and rotating test set rarely, report paired bootstrap CIs, correct for every comparison you run, and check for contamination with fresh queries the model could not have seen.

blocks.question: An LLM reranker improves nDCG@10 on a public BEIR dataset by +0.06 but shows no gain on 200 queries your team labeled last month. Which explanation should you test first?
options: The bootstrap CI on the public dataset is too narrow
Your 200 queries need Holm correction
BEIR's metric is computed incorrectly
The reranker's pretraining data may contain the public dataset, so its gain there partly reflects memorization
blocks.explain: Fresh, unpublished queries that postdate the model's training are the cleanest test. A gain that appears only on a long-public benchmark is the signature of contamination (or of distribution shift). Check overlap, for example by testing whether the model can complete the benchmark's queries or passages verbatim.

blocks.question: Which practice gives the strongest protection against both adaptive overfitting and contamination for a production search eval?
options: Averaging results over more public benchmarks
A private query set sampled from recent traffic, labeled in-house, read for a few pre-declared decisions and replaced on a schedule
Reporting results with five decimal places
Running the paired t-test with alpha = 0.01 instead of 0.05
blocks.explain: Recent private queries cannot be in a model's training data and have not been tuned against. Rotation keeps them from wearing out under repeated reads. More public benchmarks help external validity but stay exposed to contamination; stricter alpha alone does not address reuse.
